segments.text: In the 2023-24 school year, 5,359 Texas public school students were struck as punishment by an adult at school. This is a short inservice on that practice: what the law permits, where Texas districts stand, what the research finds, where the legal protections for staff stop, and what most of the state has already done instead.

Start with the statute. Texas Education Code 37.0011 defines corporal punishment as, quote, the deliberate infliction of physical pain by hitting, paddling, spanking, slapping, or any other physical force used as a means of discipline. That is the state's own language.

A board of trustees may adopt a policy permitting it. Nothing in the law requires one or recommends one. Where a policy exists, any district educator may use it on any student whose parent has not opted out.

And the opt-out is the only guardrail. A parent has to file a separate, signed statement with the board, every single school year. The statute sets no purpose, no standard of evidence, and no training requirement. It is a permission, not a recommendation. It was added in 2011.
Here is what districts themselves have reported to the federal Civil Rights Data Collection. In 2017-18, 13,892 Texas students received corporal punishment.

Down 61 percent in six years, with no change in the law. Nationally the count fell from 106,055 students a decade ago to 19,851. The practice is leaving on its own. The question for a district that still permits it is not whether to be first. It is whether to be last.

Three groups of Texas districts. 300 have written it down: the board prohibits corporal punishment. 396 still permit it on paper, but reported no use at all last year. And 284 districts reported actually using it.
Of 1,044 Texas districts in the public record, 735 still carry a policy that permits it. Most of them have already stopped in practice. The paper lags the practice.

Be fair to the policy. Its stated purpose is discipline management. The sentence most permitting Texas boards use says corporal punishment may be used as a discipline management technique in accordance with the Student Code of Conduct.

We asked the Texas Education Agency, under the Public Information Act, for any guidance, model policy, training material, research, or correspondence on corporal punishment from the last five years. The agency produced two annual discipline presentations. Each restates the statute on one slide. Neither cites a purpose, a study, or an outcome.
So the claim behind the practice is a plain one: that pain changes behavior for the better. That is a testable claim. And it has been tested.

A 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of the 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm, none toward benefit. Young adults from states where school paddling was legal had lower high school grades and more depressive symptoms. And the American Academy of Pediatrics calls it minimally effective in the short term and not effective in the long term.

Here is the counterintuitive part. The behavior the paddle is meant to stop is the behavior it is most consistently associated with producing. If a vendor sold a reading program with this evidence base, the district would cancel the contract.

Who does it land on? In Texas last year, 4,472 of the 5,359 students were boys. 83 percent. 1,186 had a disability. 22 percent. And there were 8,528 instances, so many students were struck more than once, which is its own evidence that it is not working as a deterrent.

Nationally, the U.S. Secretary of Education wrote to every governor in 2023 citing federal data that Black students were 2.3 times as likely as white students to receive corporal punishment, and Black girls four times as likely as white girls. A practice that falls hardest on boys, students with disabilities, and Black students is a civil rights exposure before it is anything else.

Now the slide for the staff in the room. The immunity statutes are real, and they are narrower than people think. Section 22.0511 says a professional employee is not personally liable for acts within the scope of the job, except, quote, in circumstances in which a professional employee uses excessive force in the discipline of students or negligence resulting in bodily injury to students.

Section 22.0512 protects your job and your certificate only for force justified under Penal Code 9.62, and it expressly lets the district discipline an employee who violates the district's own corporal punishment policy. And 9.62 justifies force only when and to the degree the actor reasonably believes it is necessary.

Every protection turns on words decided after the fact by someone else: excessive, reasonable, necessary. A missed parent opt-out is a policy violation. A bruise is a bodily-injury question. And the research you just saw is what a plaintiff's expert will use to argue the force was never necessary. This is not legal advice. Ask your district's counsel. But ask.
Before the next board meeting, put six questions to your district's risk pool or liability carrier, in writing, and keep the answers.

Is a claim arising from corporal punishment covered, excluded, or covered only within policy? Does coverage follow an employee who struck a student whose parent had filed an opt-out? Is excessive force a coverage exclusion, and who decides?

Does a federal civil rights complaint about disparate use trigger coverage? Has the pool paid or defended a corporal punishment claim in the last ten years, and at what cost? And would adopting a prohibition change the district's rate? A Kansas superintendent described the practice to us as a great way to harvest litigation. His board took it out of policy in one meeting.

When a board asks who else thinks this, here is the list. The American Academy of Pediatrics, in 2023, said corporal punishment in all school settings should be abolished in all states by law. The U.S. Secretary of Education asked every governor to end it. The school psychologists, the child psychiatrists, National PTA, and more than 100 organizations including the ACLU, the APA, both national teachers' unions, and the NAACP, all on record.
The pediatricians, the psychologists, the unions, the parents, and the federal department all landed in the same place. No professional body has taken the other side.

Here is the low-hanging fruit. The Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment in the District. One sentence. It is not ours. 291 Texas boards have already adopted it, in the same policy code, FO Local, through the same policy service your board uses.

What changes: one word. The opt-out form, the annual tracking, and the witness procedure all go away. What it costs: nothing. For the 396 districts that reported no use, Monday morning does not change at all. What it earns: the district's entry on the public record turns green, and the board receives the Safe School recognition and a press release it can use.

What works instead? A 2016 meta-analysis of 54 controlled studies found that classroom management programs improve academic, behavioral, and social-emotional outcomes, and the programs that teach social and emotional skills work best.

And none of it is new to a Texas campus. The Student Code of Conduct every district already has under Chapter 37. Campus behavior plans with taught expectations. Parent conferences and behavior contracts. In-school suspension and the D-A-E-P as the backstop the law already provides. The 300 prohibiting districts and the 396 that stopped in practice run their schools with exactly these tools. Nobody is asking your campus to adopt a new program. The ask is to stop using the one tool with no evidence behind it.

So what does this mean on your campus? If your policy prohibits it, check that the student handbook says the same thing. Dated handbook language has reached students and staff in more than one district. If your policy permits it and you do not use it, ask the board to adopt the one-sentence prohibition, and bring the six risk pool answers. It is one agenda item. If it is still in use, know who has an opt-out on file before any incident, record every instance, and know that the federal count will show it.

Your district's entry, with its own policy sentence and its source, is at earthpilot dot org slash kids slash state slash T X. If we have read it wrong, write to us and it is corrected the same day. The model language, the brief for the board, and the recognition for districts that adopt it are all free. Thank you.

Every figure in this presentation traces to one of these sources: the Texas statutes, read on the Legislature's own site; the districts' own filings to the federal Civil Rights Data Collection; the Texas Education Agency's response to our records request; and the peer-reviewed research and position statements listed here. All of it is linked at earthpilot dot org slash kids slash resources.
